lead: A periodic signal has a line spectrum. An aperiodic signal has no single period, so its spectrum becomes continuous. The Fourier transform is the limit of the exponential Fourier series as the period T₀ goes to infinity. It maps a time signal x(t) to a complex function X(ω) of angular frequency ω in rad/s. Engineers use it to see which frequencies a pulse, a transient or a message occupies, and to compute filtering, modulation and bandwidth. This chapter derives the transform, states when it exists, and builds the standard pairs used everywhere.
prereq: You need: 3.1 Fourier series and Unit 1 standard signals, plus limits from first-year calculus.

sections.h3: From Fourier series to Fourier transform

blocks.text: Start with a periodic signal x_T0(t), period T₀. Its exponential Fourier series is x_T0(t)=Σ c_n e<sup>jnω₀t</sup>, where ω₀=2π/T₀ rad/s and c_n=(1/T₀)∫x_T0(t)e<sup>−jnω₀t</sup>dt over one period. Define X_n=c_nT₀. Then x_T0(t)=(1/T₀)Σ X_n e<sup>jnω₀t</sup>. The line spacing is Δω=ω₀=2π/T₀. As T₀→∞ the signal loses its period, Δω→0, the lines merge, and the sum becomes an integral.

blocks.where: x(t) is the time signal (V if voltage); ω is angular frequency in rad/s; j=√−1; X(ω) is the complex spectrum.
X(ω) is the spectrum; dω is an infinitesimal frequency step; the factor 1/2π converts an ω integral to an f integral.

blocks.text: The integral converges if ∫|x(t)|dt<∞. Finite jumps and finite peaks are allowed. X(ω) is then continuous in ω. Some syllabi write X(jω) for the same function.
Use Sa(y)=sin y/y. The rectangular pulse rect(t/τ) equals 1 for |t|<τ/2 and 0 outside. Its transform is τSa(ωτ/2). The table lists pairs to memorise; each follows from the defining integral.

A periodic signal is not aperiodic, but its transform is still written as impulse trains: x(t)=Σ c_n e<sup>jnω₀t</sup> ↔ 2πΣ c_n δ(ω−nω₀). The impulse train Σ δ(t−nT) ↔ (2π/T)Σ δ(ω−2πn/T). These pairs let Fourier-series results sit inside the transform framework.

A signal is time-limited if x(t)=0 outside a finite interval. It is band-limited if X(ω)=0 for |ω|>B, where B is the bandwidth in rad/s. A nonzero signal cannot be both. If X(ω) is zero above B, the inverse integral runs over finite limits and produces a smooth function that cannot be zero on an interval unless it is zero everywhere. In the other direction, a rectangular pulse of width τ has a sinc spectrum with first zero at ω=2π/τ. Narrower τ gives a wider main lobe. The product τB stays roughly constant. This trade is why a short UPI confirmation burst needs more bandwidth than a steady carrier.

figure.caption: Magnitude of X(ω)=1/(2+jω) for x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t): it starts at 0.5 at ω=0 and falls to 0.354 at ω=2 rad/s.

spec.aria: The magnitude of the Fourier transform of e^{-2t}u(t) starts at 0.5 and falls as frequency rises.

examples.question: For x(t)=e<sup>−2t</sup>u(t), find X(ω). Hence find |X(ω)| at ω=0 and ω=2 rad/s.
steps: Write u(t)=1 for t≥0 and 0 for t<0, so the integral runs from 0 to ∞.
Integrate: X(ω)=[−1/(2+jω)]e<sup>−(2+jω)t</sup> evaluated from t=0 to t=∞.
At t→∞, e<sup>−2t</sup>→0 and |e<sup>−jωt</sup>|=1, so the upper limit gives 0. At t=0 the value is 1. Thus X(ω)=1/(2+jω).
examples.check:
import math
X0 = 1/math.sqrt(4+0**2)
X2 = 1/math.sqrt(4+2**2)
print(X0)
print(round(X2, 3))

traps: Forgetting the 1/(2π) factor in the inverse transform. The forward transform has no such factor in this convention.
Mixing f in Hz with ω in rad/s. Use X(ω)=∫x(t)e<sup>−jωt</sup>dt and remember ω=2πf.
Using the wrong denominator for e<sup>−at</sup>u(t). It is 1/(a+jω), not 1/(a−jω), and the lower limit is 0 because of u(t).
Assuming a time-limited pulse has a finite spectrum. A rectangular pulse has sinc tails for all ω.
Treating δ(ω−ω₀) as a finite value. It is a density with unit area; the spectrum of a sinusoid is an impulse, not a tall finite spike.

quiz.q: Write the Fourier transform and its inverse for a continuous-time signal x(t).
Why does an aperiodic signal have a continuous spectrum?
quiz.a: As T₀→∞, the harmonic spacing ω₀=2π/T₀→0. The discrete lines merge into a continuum, so the Fourier series becomes an integral over ω.

quiz.q: Find the Fourier transform of δ(t−3).
For rect(t/2), width 2 centred at 0, find X(ω) and X(0).
quiz.a: Here τ=2, so X(ω)=2Sa(ω). At ω=0, Sa(0)=1, so X(0)=2.

quiz.q: Can a nonzero signal be both time-limited and band-limited? Explain in one line.
quiz.a: No. A band-limited spectrum gives an inverse integral over finite frequencies, which cannot be zero on an interval unless the signal is zero everywhere.

quiz.q: Why is the transform of the constant 1 equal to 2πδ(ω)?
quiz.a: The inverse transform of 2πδ(ω) is (1/2π)∫2πδ(ω)e<sup>jωt</sup>dω=1 for all t.

quiz.q: A pulse is made narrower in time while its height stays fixed. What happens to its magnitude spectrum?
quiz.a: The main lobe widens and the peak value falls. The spectrum spreads over more frequencies, keeping the time-width times bandwidth product roughly constant.

beyond: Not for the exam. Continuous-time Fourier transforms underpin OFDM in 4G and 5G, radar pulse design, and spectral estimation in instrumentation. In research, the same limit idea leads to the Fourier integral theorem and to distributions such as delta functions. Search next for continuous-time Fourier transform, sinc spectrum, band-limited signal, and the Paley-Wiener theorem. Practical software computes the DFT, which samples this transform; see Unit 6.
